n-m-e1-s1-01.title: Which of the two cups has more water?
n-m-e1-s1-01.goal: Find the mistake that happens when you compare water in differently shaped containers just by how high it looks, then find a fair way to compare and make examples where height gives the wrong answer.
n-m-e1-s1-01.material: Minjae has two cups in front of him. Cup 가 is narrow and tall. Cup 나 is wide and short. Both cups have water in them, and the water in cup 가 reaches higher. Minjae wants to find out which cup has more water.
n-m-e1-s1-01.thinking.0: Telling apart what you see from what you guess
n-m-e1-s1-01.thinking.1: Moving the water to measure with the same standard and comparing
n-m-e1-s1-01.prereq.0: Knowing the shapes of containers that hold water
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s1.prompt: Minjae spoke. Pick the first line that is wrong.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, sort it as "something I saw with my eyes" or "something I guessed from what I saw".
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether a statement based on height is equally right when the two cups have the same shape and when they have different shapes.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s1.line.0: Cup 가 is narrow and tall, and cup 나 is wide and short.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s1.line.1: The water in cup 가 reaches higher than the water in cup 나.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s1.line.2: So cup 가 has more water in it.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s1.line.3: Even if the cups have different shapes, the one whose water reaches higher has more.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 say what was seen, just as it is. The first mistake is in line 3. A narrow cup fills up high with only a little water. If the cups have different shapes, you cannot tell how much water there is just by looking at the height. Line 4 stretches the idea in line 3 to apply to all cups.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the ways to compare the water in the two cups fairly.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether the amounts of water being compared were measured with the same "ruler".
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.hint.1: For each way, think about whether the shape of the cup affects the result or not.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.o.a: Pour the water from each cup into two identical empty bottles and compare the heights
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.r.a: Put the two cups side by side and look at them carefully for a longer time
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.o.b: Scoop the water out of each cup with a small dish and count how many scoops
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.r.b: Decide that the cup with the bigger outside shape has more water
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.o.c: If you pour the water into containers of the same shape, you can compare by height. That is a good way, because the shapes are made the same.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.r.c: Looking for longer does not get rid of the illusion caused by the shapes. You need a way to measure with the same standard.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.o.d: This counts how many times the same small container is filled. You can compare no matter what shape the cups are.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.r.d: A big cup may hold only a little water. You have to compare the water inside directly.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s2.explain: You cannot compare the water in differently shaped cups just by looking at the height. If you pour it into identical empty bottles and compare the heights, or count how many scoops of the same small dish it takes, you can compare fairly.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.prompt: When scooping with a small dish, the water in cup 가 took a scoops and the water in cup 나 took b scoops. Make three different cases where the water in cup 가 reaches higher but cup 나 has more water, by changing a and b. a and b are numbers from 1 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.hint.0: The side with the bigger number of scoops has more water. First decide which cup should have the bigger number of scoops.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.hint.1: Pick a, then choose b as a number bigger than a. Then change to a different a and do it again.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.var.a: Water in cup 가 (how many scoops) a
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.var.b: Water in cup 나 (how many scoops) b
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.ok.c1: a is a number from 1 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make a a number from 1 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.ok.c2: b is a number from 1 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.fail.c2: Please make b a number from 1 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.ok.c3: Cup 나 has more water (its number of scoops is bigger).
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.fail.c3: For cup 나 to have more water, its number of scoops must be bigger than that of cup 가.
n-m-e1-s1-01.s.s3.explain: The more scoops it takes, the more water there is. For example, if cup 가 takes 2 scoops and cup 나 takes 5 scoops, cup 나 has more water even though the water in cup 가 reaches higher. So there are many examples where height alone gives the wrong answer.

n-m-e1-s1-02.title: Ways to split 8 candies between two plates
n-m-e1-s1-02.topic: Addition and subtraction: splitting and combining numbers
n-m-e1-s1-02.goal: Find every way to split a number into two numbers, in an order so that none is missed, and use the rules to judge cases where the two numbers are the same or a plate is empty.
n-m-e1-s1-02.material: Harin wants to put 8 candies onto two plates. Putting 3 on one plate and 5 on the other is called "splitting into 3 and 5". Swapping the plates and putting 5 and 3 counts as the same split. Even if both plates have the same number, it is still a split.
n-m-e1-s1-02.thinking.1: Checking whether it fits the rules (conditions)
n-m-e1-s1-02.prereq.1: Knowing what numbers make when put together
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the ways to put 8 candies onto two plates. Each plate must have at least 1 candy.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each way, combine the candies on the two plates and check whether they make 8.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.hint.1: Also check one by one whether each way fits the rule that each plate has at least 1.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.o.a: 0 on one plate, 8 on the other
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.r.a: One plate is empty. It does not fit the rule that each plate has at least 1.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.o.b: 4 on one plate, 4 on the other
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.r.b: Even if the two plates have the same number, it is still a split. Check whether the total is 8.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.o.c: 3 on one plate, 4 on the other
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.r.c: 3 and 4 put together make 7. One candy is missing.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.o.d: 2 on one plate, 6 on the other
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.r.d: This is a split whose total is 8. This way fits the rules too.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s1.explain: 4 and 4, and 2 and 6, make 8 when put together and each plate has at least 1, so they work. 0 and 8 does not work because one plate is empty, and 3 and 4 does not work because they make 7. 4 and 4, with the same number on both plates, is also a split.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.prompt: Find three different ways to split 8 into two numbers. Let the smaller number be a and the larger number be b. If the two numbers are the same, write the same number for a and b. Count 3 and 5, and 5 and 3, as the same split.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write one split first, then look at what happens to the other number when one number goes up by 1.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.hint.1: For each split you found, check that the two numbers make 8 together and that you wrote the smaller one as a.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.ok.c1: a is a number that is 1 or more.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a must be 1 or more. A plate must not be empty.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.ok.c2: b is a number counted in single candies.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.fail.c2: b is a number of candies, so it must be counted in ones.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.ok.c3: a is less than or equal to b.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.fail.c3: a must be the smaller number. Write it so that a is not greater than b.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.fail.c4: The two numbers do not make 8 together.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s2.explain: You can find 1 and 7, 2 and 6, 3 and 5, and 4 and 4. 5 and 3 is just 3 and 5 with the plates swapped, so it is the same split.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.prompt: What is a good way to find every split of 8 without missing any?
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.hint.0: Line up the three you found in the order you wrote them and see whether there was a pattern.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.hint.1: After finding one split, think back to how you found the next one.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.o.a: Write whatever comes to mind and stop when nothing else comes
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.r.a: If you write only what comes to mind, it is hard to tell even when a split is missing.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.o.b: Set one number starting from 1 in order, find the other, and stop when the two numbers become the same
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.r.b: If you go in order, you can check right away that nothing is missing.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.o.c: Pick big numbers first in any order you like and write the splits
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.r.c: If you pick in any order, it is hard to see which splits you wrote or missed.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.o.d: Split only into two different numbers and leave out the same number
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.r.d: 4 and 4 is a split too. You missed the case of splitting into the same number.
n-m-e1-s1-02.s.s3.explain: If you set one number in order starting from 1 and find the other, you will not miss any. If you stop where the two numbers become the same (4 and 4), the same split will not appear twice.

n-m-e1-s1-03.title: How many candies does Seoyun have in all?
n-m-e1-s1-03.topic: Numbers up to 50: ten-blocks and two-digit numbers
n-m-e1-s1-03.goal: Work out what you need to know to find the number of items when the counting units are different, like bags and single pieces, and when there are more than 10 single pieces, turn them into a bundle and write the number as tens and ones.
n-m-e1-s1-03.material: Seoyun has 3 bags of candy and 7 single candies. She wants to know how many candies she has in all.
n-m-e1-s1-03.thinking.1: Numbers with different units cannot be added right away
n-m-e1-s1-03.thinking.2: Changing 10 single pieces into one bundle
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.prompt: What must you know to find how many candies Seoyun has in all?
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write down separately what the story has already told you and what it has not told you yet.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what is inside a bag, and think about how many candies one bag should be counted as.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.r.a: The bag color has nothing to do with the number of candies.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.o.b: How many candies are in one bag
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.r.b: You need to know how many are in one bag to count the candies inside the bags.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.o.c: Nothing more is needed, just add 3 and 7
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.r.c: 3 bags and 7 single pieces are not the same kind of number. Think about whether one bag is one candy.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.o.d: How many single candies there are
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.r.d: You already know there are 7 single pieces. Look for what you do not know yet.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s1.explain: If you do not know how many candies are in one bag, you cannot count the candies in the 3 bags. 3 bags and 7 single pieces are different things being counted, so you cannot simply add them.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s2.prompt: Seoyun said, "There are 10 candies in every bag. They are all the same." Then how many candies does Seoyun have in all?
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s2.hint.0: Count the 3 bags in bundles of 10. You may also skip count 10, 20, ...
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s2.hint.1: Count the candies in the bags first, and then add the single pieces.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s2.r.a: This treats 10, the sum of 3 bags and 7 single pieces, as the number of candies. It did not use the fact that one bag has 10 candies.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s2.r.b: The number of bags and the number of single pieces were put the wrong way around. Look again at how many bags and how many single pieces there are.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s2.r.c: The number of bundles of 10 was put in the 100s place. If one bag is 10 candies, count how many candies 3 bags are.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s2.r.d: 3 bags are 30 candies, and adding 7 single pieces makes 37. It is the same as 3 ten-blocks and 7 ones.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s2.explain: One bag is 10, so 3 bags are 30. Adding 7 single pieces makes 37. It is the same as laying out 3 ten-blocks and 7 ones.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s3.prompt: Seoyun got 5 more single candies. Now she has 12 single candies. How many candies does Seoyun have in all now?
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s3.hint.0: Bundle the 12 single pieces in 10s. See how many bundles there are and how many single pieces are left.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s3.hint.1: Draw ten-blocks, showing bundles as bars and single pieces as dots, and count.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s3.r.a: If you bundle 10 of the 12 single pieces like a new bag, you get 4 bundles and 2 single pieces.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s3.r.b: This puts 3 and 12 side by side. 12 single pieces cannot be written in one place.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s3.r.c: This adds the 3 bags and the 12 single pieces. Think about how many candies one bag has.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s3.r.d: This missed bundling 10 of the 12 single pieces. When there are 10 single pieces, they become one bundle.
n-m-e1-s1-03.s.s3.explain: 3 bags are 30, and adding 12 single pieces makes 42. 12 single pieces can be seen as one bundle of 10 and 2 single pieces, so that makes 4 bundles and 2 single pieces, which is 42.

n-m-e1-s1-04.title: Testing Seoyeon's claim
n-m-e1-s1-04.topic: Numbers up to 9 and addition and subtraction: adding and subtracting 0
n-m-e1-s1-04.goal: Test the claim "adding always makes it bigger and subtracting always makes it smaller" with examples, find that the case of 0 is a counterexample, and explain why in words.
n-m-e1-s1-04.material: Seoyeon said, "When you add to a number, it always gets bigger than it was, and when you subtract, it always gets smaller than it was." You want to find out whether Seoyeon is right. Only use numbers from 0 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-04.thinking.2: Testing the claim "it is always so"
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the expressions that can show Seoyeon's claim is wrong.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s1.hint.0: First write down what the result should be if Seoyeon is right, then compare the result of each expression with the starting number.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the starting number and the result would look in an expression that goes against Seoyeon's claim.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s1.r.a: Even though the starting number is 0, adding 3 made it bigger, 3. It does not go against Seoyeon's claim.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s1.r.b: Adding 0 did not make it bigger. It is an example that goes against Seoyeon's claim.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s1.r.c: Subtracting made it smaller, 5. It does not go against Seoyeon's claim.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s1.r.d: Subtracting 0 did not make it smaller. It is an example that goes against Seoyeon's claim.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s1.r.e: Subtracting made it smaller, 0. It does not go against Seoyeon's claim.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s1.explain: In 6+0=6 we added but it did not get bigger, and in 8-0=8 we subtracted but it did not get smaller. Even one such example makes the claim "it is always so" wrong. No matter how many examples agree with Seoyeon's claim, you cannot say the claim is right.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.prompt: Find cases where adding the same number b to a number a gives the same result as subtracting b from a. a is a number from 1 to 9, and b is a number from 0 to 9. Change a and write three different cases.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.hint.0: Change b to 0, 1, and 2, and work out both a+b and a-b.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.hint.1: Once you find a b that makes the two results the same, try other values of a with the same b.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.ok.c1: a is a number from 1 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a a number from 1 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.ok.c2: b is a number from 0 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make b a number from 0 to 9.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.ok.c3: a+b and a-b are the same.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c3: a+b and a-b are not the same. The result of adding and the result of subtracting came out different.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s2.explain: Adding and subtracting give the same result only when b is 0. 4+0=4 and 4-0=4. No matter what a is, it is always so when b is 0.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.prompt: Tell Seoyeon. Write when the number stays the same after adding or subtracting, along with the reason.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write the expressions you found in s2 side by side and find what each one has in common.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine what it actually means to add or subtract that number, and say how the result compares with the starting number.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say when it stays the same after adding or subtracting?
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the reason with the words "nothing was added or subtracted"?
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it in words that Seoyeon can easily understand?
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.model.0: If you add or subtract 0, the number stays the same. Like 4+0=4 and 4-0=4, because nothing is added or subtracted.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.model.1: If you add 0, which is nothing, it is the same as the starting number. Subtracting is the same. 6+0 is 6 and 6-0 is 6.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.model.2: When the number you add is zero, it does not get bigger and stays the same. When the number you subtract is zero, it does not get smaller and stays the same.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.model.3: If the number you add is 0, it does not get bigger. That is because nothing was added.
n-m-e1-s1-04.s.s3.model.4: If there is nothing to subtract, it stays the same. If you subtract nothing from 8, it is still 8.

n-m-e1-s1-05.title: My own way to sort objects
n-m-e1-s1-05.goal: Learn about sorting rules that give the same result no matter who uses them, sort everyday objects with your own rule, and check that the rule is applied to every part of an object.
n-m-e1-s1-05.material: On the desk there are a die, a snack box, a can of food, a baseball, and a marble. You want to sort these five objects into two groups. Even if people use the same rule, the groups must not come out differently from person to person.
n-m-e1-s1-05.thinking.1: Applying the rule the same way in every case
n-m-e1-s1-05.thinking.2: Recognizing rules that change from person to person
n-m-e1-s1-05.prereq.0: Recognizing box shapes, cylinder shapes, and ball shapes
n-m-e1-s1-05.prereq.1: Sorting by saying "has it / does not have it"
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.prompt: You want to sort the die, snack box, can of food, baseball, and marble into two groups. Choose all the rules that always sort the same way, whether you or a friend sorts separately.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.hint.0: Pick one rule and sort all five objects. Is it clear right away which object goes in which group?
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine a friend using the same rule and think about whether the friend would sort them the same way.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.o.a: Those that have a flat face and those that have none
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.r.a: If you feel each object for a flat face, anyone can sort them the same way.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.o.b: Pretty ones and not pretty ones
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.r.b: What people think is pretty is different for each person. You and a friend could sort differently.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.r.c: Where "big" stops is different for each person. It is hard to decide which side the baseball or the can belongs to.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.o.d: Those that have a round part and those that have none
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.r.d: If you feel each object for a round part, anyone can sort them the same way.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s1.explain: The rule has to give the same answer no matter who touches or looks at the objects, so that they are sorted the same way. Whether there is a flat face or a round part can be decided by looking at the object. Being pretty or big can change from person to person.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.prompt: This time, choose a rule of your own and sort the five objects (die, snack box, can of food, baseball, marble) into two groups. Write the rule and the names of the objects in each group.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine holding the five objects one by one, and find one thing you can tell by looking or touching.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.hint.1: With your rule, say which group each object goes in, and see whether any object makes you hesitate.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.placeholder: For example: The rule is ... Those that are ... are ..., and those that are not are ...
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is it a rule that sorts the same way no matter who does it?
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you put all five objects in one of the two groups?
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Is neither of the two groups empty?
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.model.0: The rule is whether there is a round part. Those that have one are the can, baseball, and marble, and those that do not are the die and the snack box.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.model.1: The ones with pointy corners are the die and the snack box, and the ones without corners are the can, baseball, and marble.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.model.2: I sorted by whether it rolls in any direction. The baseball and the marble roll anywhere, and the die, snack box, and can do not.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s2.model.3: I sorted by whether it bounces when thrown. The ones that bounce are the baseball and the marble, and the ones that do not are the die, snack box, and can.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s3.prompt: Seojun also sorted by "whether there is a flat face". Pick the one line that is wrong in Seojun's explanation.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s3.hint.0: For each line, think of the object Seojun mentioned and check one by one whether it fits Seojun's rule.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine holding one object and feeling every side of it, and read the lines again.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s3.line.0: I sorted by whether there is a flat face.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s3.line.1: The die has a flat face, so it is in the "has one" group.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s3.line.2: The snack box also has a flat face, so it is in the "has one" group.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s3.line.3: The can has a round side, so it is in the "has none" group.
n-m-e1-s1-05.s.s3.line.4: The baseball and the marble have no flat face, so they are in the "has none" group.

n-m-e1-s2-02.title: If the sum of two digits is even, is the number even too?
n-m-e1-s2-02.topic: Numbers up to 100: even and odd numbers
n-m-e1-s2-02.goal: Check with a counterexample that a claim is not always right even if a few examples fit, and say, with a reason, which place decides whether a two-digit number is even.
n-m-e1-s2-02.material: When you pair things up two by two and nothing is left over, the number is "even", and when one is left over, it is "odd". Doyun says he found an easy way to tell whether a two-digit number is even. Doyun's claim is this: "If you add the two digits and get an even number, then the number is even too." Doyun's examples are 22 and 46. 2+2=4 and 4+6=10, and 22 and 46 are both even.
n-m-e1-s2-02.thinking.0: Deciding whether a few examples are enough to trust the whole claim
n-m-e1-s2-02.thinking.1: Making an example where the claim is wrong (a counterexample)
n-m-e1-s2-02.thinking.2: Explaining which place decides whether a number is even, and why
n-m-e1-s2-02.prereq.0: Meaning of even and odd (pairing two by two and seeing if one is left, Grade 1 level)
n-m-e1-s2-02.prereq.1: Knowing the tens place and ones place of a two-digit number
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.prompt: What is a good way to find out whether Doyun's claim is always right?
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.hint.0: First say in words which numbers Doyun's claim is about.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.hint.1: Find a few more such numbers and see whether any of them goes against the claim.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.o.a: 22 and 46 worked, so there is no need to look at more
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.r.a: Think about whether two examples working means it works for all numbers.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.o.b: Pick any number other than 22 and 46 and look at it
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.r.b: Doyun's claim is about numbers whose digit sum is even. If you pick any number, you may not be testing the claim.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.o.c: Find and look at more numbers whose digit sum is even
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.r.c: To test Doyun's claim, it is good to look for more of the numbers the claim is about.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.r.d: Calculating examples that already worked again tells you nothing new.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s1.explain: Doyun's claim is about "numbers whose two digits add up to an even number". You have to find more such numbers and check whether they are even to know whether the claim is always right.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s2.prompt: Find three different cases where Doyun's claim is wrong. Choose a two-digit number n whose two digits add up to an even number but n itself is odd.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a two-digit number, then write its tens digit and ones digit separately and add them.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s2.hint.1: When the sum is even, set out that many marbles as the number you chose, pair them up two by two, and check whether one is left.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make n a natural number from 10 to 99.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The two digits add up to an even number.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The two digits do not add up to an even number. Add the tens digit and the ones digit.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s2.fail.c3: n is not odd. It should be a number that leaves one over when marbles are paired two by two.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s2.explain: 13 has 1+3=4, so the sum is even, but 13 is odd. So are 35, 91, and 57. When the tens digit and the ones digit are both odd, the number goes against Doyun's claim.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.prompt: Tell Doyun. Write which place's digit you should look at to find out whether a two-digit number is even, and why, giving an example.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.hint.0: In the numbers you checked earlier for even and odd, look at where the leftover marble comes from.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.hint.1: Try pairing up 10 marbles two by two to see if any are left, and think of a two-digit number as bundles and single pieces.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.placeholder: For example: Doyun, you can look at the ... place. That is because ...
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the ones place and the tens place separately?
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write why bundles of 10 pair up evenly?
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you show the number you chose as an example?
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.model.0: Doyun, look at the ones place. Bundles of 10 pair up two by two exactly, so only the single pieces can be left over. 13 has 3 single pieces left, so it is odd.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.model.1: You do not need to look at the tens place. If the ones place is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, the number is even. That is because 10 can be paired up two by two. 24 is even because 4 is even.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: Written with the words "you don't need to look".
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.model.2: If the rightmost digit is even, the number is even. The tens place is bundles of 10, so they always pair up. For example, 57 is odd because 7 is odd.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.model.3: Just look at the last digit. 46 is even because 6 is even. Bundles of 10 can be paired up two by two.
n-m-e1-s2-02.s.s3.model.4: If the ones place is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, it is even. That is because 10 can be split in two. For example, 38 is even because 8 is even.

n-m-e1-s2-03.title: Why carrying happens, explained to a younger sibling
n-m-e1-s2-03.goal: Explain with marble pictures that when there are 10 single pieces they become one bundle of 10, make additions that need carrying, and write the reason in words a younger sibling can understand.
n-m-e1-s2-03.material: Seoa has 27 marbles. That is 2 bundles of 10 and 7 single marbles. Seoa got 5 more marbles. Her younger sibling asked, "How do you work out 27+5?" Seoa wants to show and explain it with marbles.
n-m-e1-s2-03.thinking.0: Showing a calculation method with marbles (bundles and single pieces)
n-m-e1-s2-03.thinking.1: Making and checking the boundary case (exactly 10) where carrying happens
n-m-e1-s2-03.thinking.2: Rewording the same idea at a young child's level
n-m-e1-s2-03.prereq.0: Showing a two-digit number as bundles of 10 and single pieces (Grade 1 level)
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s1.prompt: Seoa's 27 marbles are 2 bundles of 10 and 7 single marbles. Adding 5 to the 7 single marbles makes 12 single marbles. What happens if you bundle these 12 single marbles in 10s?
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s1.hint.0: Draw 12 marbles and circle groups of 10.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s1.hint.1: Count the marbles inside the circle and the marbles left outside separately.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s1.r.a: This misses that single pieces over 10 can be bundled.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s1.r.b: This split 12 into its tens digit and ones digit and then read them the wrong way around.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s1.r.c: This counted as if the single pieces stayed after bundling. Take the bundled 10 away from the single pieces.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s1.r.d: This split the 12 single marbles into a bundle and single pieces and counted.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s1.explain: If you bundle 10 out of 12 single marbles, you get 1 bundle of 10, and 2 single marbles are left.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s2.prompt: Make three different additions where the single pieces add up to exactly 10. Add a one-digit number b to a two-digit number a. The ones digit of a plus b must make 10.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s2.hint.0: Pick the ones digit of a, then count with marbles what b must be to make 10 single pieces.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s2.hint.1: Work out the expression you made and check what the ones place becomes.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a a natural number from 10 to 99.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make b a natural number from 1 to 9.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The single pieces add up to exactly 10.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The ones digit of a plus b does not make 10. There are fewer or more than 10 single pieces.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s2.explain: In 23+7, 48+2, and 65+5, when the single pieces make exactly 10, there is 1 more bundle of 10 and no single pieces are left over.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.prompt: You want to explain it to your younger sibling. In 23+7=30, write why you put 0 in the ones place and the tens digit goes up by one, thinking of marbles and talking as if to your sibling.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.hint.0: Draw 23 and 7 with marbles, gather the single pieces in one place, and count how many there are.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.hint.1: After gathering the single pieces, think about what is left in the ones place and the tens place when you bundle them in 10s.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.placeholder: For example: 23 is 2 bundles of 10 and 3 single marbles, and ...

n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say that 10 single pieces change into one bundle of 10?
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it in words your sibling can easily understand?
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.model.0: If you add 7 to 23, the single marbles are 3 and 7, so there are 10. 10 single marbles make one bundle of 10, so no single marbles are left, and there is one more bundle, so the tens place goes from 2 to 3.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.model.1: With marbles, if you add 7 to 3 single marbles, you get ten. If you tie ten into one bundle, there are 0 single marbles and one more bundle of 10, so 20 becomes 30.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.model.2: Add the ones digits 3 and 7 and you get 10. 10 is one bundle of 10, so it goes to the tens place, and you only write 0 in the ones place.
n-m-e1-s2-03.s.s3.model.3: Since 3+7=10, the ones place is 0, and the 10 goes up to the tens place.

n-m-e1-s2-04.title: Checking Jiho's answer for 42-9
n-m-e1-s2-04.goal: Find and fix the mistake of subtracting upside down when there are not enough single pieces, learn how to check a subtraction answer by looking back, and make an expression that needs borrowing yourself.
n-m-e1-s2-04.material: Jiho worked out 42-9. There were 42 marbles and 9 were used. Jiho started from the ones place. Below is the story of Jiho's calculation.
n-m-e1-s2-04.thinking.0: Finding the first place the calculation went wrong
n-m-e1-s2-04.thinking.1: Choosing a way to check whether the answer is right (comparing with the starting number, adding back)
n-m-e1-s2-04.thinking.2: Making a case that needs borrowing yourself
n-m-e1-s2-04.prereq.0: Showing a two-digit number as bundles of 10 and single pieces (Grade 1 level)
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s1.prompt: Pick the first line in Jiho's story that is wrong.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s1.hint.0: Draw 42 marbles as 4 bundles of 10 and 2 single marbles, and then try to take 9 away from the 2 single marbles.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s1.hint.1: When there are not enough single pieces, think about what to do by moving the marbles yourself.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s1.line.0: 42 is 4 bundles of 10 and 2 single marbles.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s1.line.1: You cannot take 9 away from 2 single marbles.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s1.line.2: So subtract 2 from 9 and write 7 single marbles.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s1.line.3: Leave the 4 bundles of 10 as they are.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 and 2 are correct. In line 3, Jiho could not subtract, so he turned it around and subtracted 2 from 9. When the ones are not enough, you break one bundle of 10 into 10 ones and subtract 9 from 12. Then 3 bundles are left. Lines 4 and 5 carried on from the wrong line.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the ways to check whether Jiho's answer 47 is correct.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.hint.0: There were 42 marbles and 9 were used. Think about whether the marbles left will be more or fewer than at the start.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.hint.1: If the answer is correct, think about what should happen when you put the marbles left and the marbles used together, and try adding them yourself.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.r.a: If you subtract the number being taken away from the answer again, you do not get back the starting number. Think about putting together the marbles used and the marbles left.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.o.b: Add 47 and 9 and see whether you get 42.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.r.b: This is a way to check whether the marbles left and the marbles used together make the number of marbles at the start.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.o.c: See whether the answer 47 is less than the starting number 42.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.r.c: This uses the fact that after marbles are used, there must be fewer marbles left than at the start.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.r.d: If you add the number used to the starting number, you get the number for a different situation. It has nothing to do with whether the answer is correct.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.explain: The answer to a subtraction must be less than the starting number. Also, if you add the number subtracted to the answer, you must get the starting number. 47+9=56 is not 42, and 47 is greater than 42, so it looks wrong.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.acc.0: Checking whether adding gives the starting number is a good way to check. You can also use the way of seeing whether the answer is less than the starting number.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s2.acc.1: Noticing that the answer to a subtraction must be less than the starting number is a good check. But being less is not enough to be correct, so also check whether adding gives the starting number.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s3.prompt: This time, make three different subtractions where the ones are not enough, so you have to break one bundle of 10, and calculate and write the answers. Subtract a one-digit number b from a two-digit number a, and the answer is c.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s3.hint.0: Decide the ones digit of a, then choose a one-digit number b that is greater than it, so that there are not enough ones.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s3.hint.1: Break one bundle of 10 into 10 ones and calculate. Then add b to the answer and check whether you get a.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make a a natural number from 10 to 99.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s3.fail.c2: Please make b a natural number from 1 to 9.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s3.ok.c3: The ones are not enough, so a bundle of 10 has to be broken.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s3.fail.c3: You can subtract b from the ones of a, so there is no need to break a bundle.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s3.fail.c4: The answer is not correct. Break one bundle of 10 into 10 ones and calculate again.
n-m-e1-s2-04.s.s3.explain: In 42-9, if you break one of the 4 bundles of 10, you get 3 bundles and 12 ones. 12-9=3, so the answer is 33.

n-m-e1-s2-05.title: When the Short Hand Is Between Two Numbers
n-m-e1-s2-05.topic: Shapes and time: __:30 (when the short hand is between numbers)
n-m-e1-s2-05.goal: Each time you see a new clock, test your rule for reading the hour. Learn that you must read the number the short hand has just passed for it to work in every case, and correct a friend's wrongly read time.

n-m-e1-s2-05.thinking.1: Notice a case where a rule that looked right at first breaks

n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s1.st.2.after: The short hand has passed 12 and is moving toward 1, so it is 12:30. The rule of reading the smaller number does not work on this clock. The rule of reading the number just passed works on every clock seen so far.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This thinking used the rule of reading the smaller of the two numbers. Look at which number the short hand has passed.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This thinking read the number the short hand has just passed.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This thinking mistook the number just before where the short hand is for 11.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: I cannot read whether it is 1:30 or 12:30.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This thinking put off deciding without choosing a rule to read with.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s1.reflect: At first, you made rules with two o'clock clocks, and on clocks with the short hand between numbers, both rules seemed to work equally well. But on the clock between 12 and 1, the rule of reading the smaller number broke. You can only know which rule always works by testing whether it works on new cases too. Tell where your thinking changed.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s2.prompt: The long hand is pointing to 6. Choose all the times that are read correctly from the position of the short hand.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s2.hint.0: Draw each clock and mark with an arrow which number the short hand has passed and which number it is moving toward.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s2.hint.1: Tell apart the number the short hand has not reached yet from the number it has already passed.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s2.r.a: The short hand has passed 6 and is moving toward 7, so it is 6:30. You read the number just passed.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s2.r.b: The short hand has not reached 10 yet. Find the number it has just passed.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s2.r.c: The short hand has passed 11 and is moving toward 12, so it is 11:30. You read the number just passed.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s2.r.d: The short hand has not reached 3 yet. Find the number it has just passed.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s2.explain: When the long hand is at 6, the short hand is exactly halfway between two numbers. The number the short hand has just passed is the hour. So 6:30 and 11:30 are correct, while between 9 and 10 it is 9:30, and between 2 and 3 it is 2:30.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.prompt: Minho said, 'The short hand is between 4 and 5 and the long hand is on 6, so it is 5:30.' What would be a good thing to say to Minho?
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.hint.0: Draw the short hand between 4 and 5, and draw an arrow showing which number it has passed and which number it is moving toward.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.hint.1: Think about where the long hand should be for it to be 5 o'clock, and compare it with the clock now.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you clearly write the __:30 time as numbers?
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the reason, which number the short hand has passed?
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write in words that are easy for Minho to understand?
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.model.0: Minho, the short hand has passed 4 and is moving toward 5. It has not reached 5 yet, so it is 4:30.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.model.1: It is 4:30. The short hand has not arrived at 5 yet. For it to be 5 o'clock, the long hand has to go all the way around to 12.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.model.2: The short hand is halfway between 4 and 5 and has passed 4, so you should read it as four thirty.
n-m-e1-s2-05.s.s3.modelNote.2: The numbers were written in words.

n-m-e1-s2b-01.title: Is It the Same Rule If the Shapes Change?
n-m-e1-s2b-01.goal: Learn that even if the shapes used change, it is the same rule when the same shapes are in the same places, and make several rows with the same rule.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.material: Seoa put shape cards in one row: '○ □ □ ○ □ □ ○ □ □'. The cards are ○, □, and △. We want to find rows that have 'the same rule' as Seoa's row.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.thinking.0: Think about what 'the same rule' means
n-m-e1-s2b-01.thinking.1: Make and check rows where the shapes are swapped
n-m-e1-s2b-01.thinking.2: Describe the rule by the pattern of places, not by the shapes
n-m-e1-s2b-01.prereq.1: Explaining a repeating rule in words (1st-grade level)
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the rows that have the same rule as Seoa's row '○ □ □ ○ □ □ ○ □ □'.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine coloring the same shapes in Seoa's row with the same colored pencil, and write down which places the same shape comes in.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s1.hint.1: Mark the same shapes in each row the same way, and compare whether the places are exactly the same as in Seoa's row.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s1.r.a: There are three kinds of shapes, and the pattern repeats every three cards. Seoa's row has two kinds of shapes.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s1.r.c: The same shapes come in pairs. Compare with the places where the same shapes sit in Seoa's row.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s1.r.e: Two shapes alternate one at a time. In Seoa's row, there are places where the same shape comes twice in a row.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s1.explain: Seoa's row repeats 'one shape followed by two of another shape in a row'. △ □ □ △ □ □ and □ ○ ○ □ ○ ○ have the same pattern too. Even if the kinds of shapes are different, it is the same rule if the same shapes are in the same places.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.prompt: Let ○ be 1, □ be 2, and △ be 3. Make rows with the same rule as Seoa's row. Write the first card as a, the second as b, the third as c, and the fourth as d. Make three different rows.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.hint.0: In Seoa's row ○ □ □ ○, first find which positions the same cards come in.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose two shapes and place them so that the same shapes come in the same places as in Seoa's row. Lay your finished row over Seoa's row and compare.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.ok.c1: You used 1, 2, or 3 for the cards.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.fail.c1: You can only use 1, 2, or 3 for the cards.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The first and second cards are different.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.fail.c2: In Seoa's row, the first and second cards are different.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The second and third cards are the same.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.fail.c3: In Seoa's row, the second and third cards are the same. Compare with Seoa's row.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.ok.c4: The fourth card is the same as the first card, so the rule starts over.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.fail.c4: Look again at which card the fourth card is the same as in Seoa's row.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s2.explain: If the first and second cards are different, the second and third are the same, and the fourth is the same as the first again, as in ○ □ □ ○, △ ○ ○ △, and □ △ △ □, it is the same rule as Seoa's row. There are six rows in all that you can make by swapping the shapes.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s3.prompt: '○ □ □ ○ □ □' and '△ ○ ○ △ ○ ○' use different shapes. Even so, why can we say they have the same rule?
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s3.hint.0: Put the two rows one above the other and draw connecting lines between the same shapes.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether the connecting lines start and end in the same places.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s3.o.a: The shapes used are different, so the rules are different.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s3.r.a: Even if you swap the shapes, if the same shapes are in the same places, you can see it as the same rule. Think back to the rows you made earlier.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s3.r.b: Even if the number of shapes is the same, the rules can be different. ○ □ ○ □ ○ □ also has 6.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s3.o.c: One shape is followed by two of the same shape, and this repeats.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s3.r.d: Just containing the same shape does not mean the rules are the same. Look at the places where the same shapes sit.
n-m-e1-s2b-01.s.s3.explain: In both rows, 'one shape, then two of another shape' repeats. The rule depends not on which shapes are used, but on which places the same shapes are in.

n-m-e1-s2b-02.title: After How Many Cards Will the Picture Cards Look the Same?
n-m-e1-s2b-02.goal: In a rule where two things change together, such as shape and color, check by drawing cards that one thing repeating does not mean the whole card repeats.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.material: Jiho is laying picture cards in one row. The shapes alternate between ○ and □, and the colors go around red, blue, yellow in order. The 1st is a red ○, the 2nd is a blue □, and the 3rd is a yellow ○. Jiho said, 'The colors repeat every three cards, so the same card will come every three cards.'
n-m-e1-s2b-02.thinking.0: Check a claim that looks at only one feature and speaks about the whole
n-m-e1-s2b-02.thinking.1: Find a counterexample by laying out the cards yourself
n-m-e1-s2b-02.thinking.2: Compare how long it takes each of the two rules to come around
n-m-e1-s2b-02.prereq.0: Reading the color rule and the shape rule separately
n-m-e1-s2b-02.prereq.1: Knowing words for order (which one: first, second, ...)
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.prompt: What do you think about what Jiho said? Draw the 4th card following the rules, and decide.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write only the colors of cards 1 to 4 first, and then write only the shapes separately.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.hint.1: Put the 4th card next to the 1st card and compare the color and the shape one at a time.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.o.a: Right. The 4th card will also be a red ○.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.r.a: Think back on whether you decided the color and the shape of the 4th card separately. The shape changes every two cards.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.o.b: Wrong. The 4th card is red, but its shape is □.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.o.c: Wrong. The rule for how the colors go around is wrong from the start.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.r.c: The color rule is just as the problem told you. Check the reason you said it was wrong using the 4th card.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.o.d: I cannot tell. I would have to lay out more cards.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.r.d: The rules are set, so you can tell what the 4th card is. Continue the colors and the shapes each in turn.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s1.explain: The color of the 4th card comes back to red, but the shapes alternate ○, □, ○, □, so it is □. So the 4th card is not the same as the 1st card. One thing being the same does not make the whole card the same.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s2.prompt: At which number does a card that has both the same color and the same shape as the 1st card appear for the first time?
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s2.hint.0: Draw the cards up to the 7th. Under each number, write the color and the shape together.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s2.hint.1: Circle the cards that have both the same color and the same shape as the 1st card.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s2.r.a: The 3rd card is yellow. Check whether the color is different.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s2.r.b: The 4th card has a different shape. Think back to what you checked earlier.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s2.r.c: Compare the color and the shape of the 6th card with the 1st.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s2.explain: If you lay out the cards in order, they are red ○, blue □, yellow ○, red □, blue ○, yellow □, red ○. The 7th is the first card that looks exactly like the 1st. The colors come back every 3 cards and the shapes every 2 cards, so for both to come back together it takes 6 cards.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s3.prompt: This time the shapes alternate between ○ and □, and the colors alternate between red and blue. The 1st is a red ○ and the 2nd is a blue □. After how many cards will the same card repeat?
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s3.hint.0: Draw the 3rd and 4th cards and compare them with the 1st and 2nd cards.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s3.hint.1: Write down separately how many cards it takes for the shapes to come back and for the colors to come back, and compare them.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s3.r.b: This thinking took the 3 cards from the previous problem as they were. Draw the 3rd card of this row yourself.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s3.r.c: This thinking added 2 cards for the shapes and 2 cards for the colors. Check how the 3rd card compares with the 1st.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s3.r.d: This thinking took the 6 cards from the previous problem as they were. In this row, the length of the rule is different.
n-m-e1-s2b-02.s.s3.explain: Both the shapes and the colors come back every 2 cards, so the 3rd card is a red ○, exactly the same as the 1st. If the two rules come back after the same length, the cards repeat after that length. If the lengths are different (2 and 3 earlier), it takes longer.

n-m-e1-s2b-03.title: Counting a String of Beads by Color
n-m-e1-s2b-03.goal: When a string with a repeating color rule ends in the middle of one set of the rule, learn that the beads left over at the end must also be counted by color, and look at how the number of each color changes with the number of beads.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.material: Minho strung 8 beads like this: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, red, blue. Minho wants to find out how many red beads and how many blue beads there are. Below is Minho's solution.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.thinking.0: Find and fix the wrong line in a solution
n-m-e1-s2b-03.thinking.1: Count the part left over at the end separately
n-m-e1-s2b-03.thinking.2: Find several different numbers that fit a condition
n-m-e1-s2b-03.prereq.0: Reading a string of beads with a red, blue rule
n-m-e1-s2b-03.prereq.1: Counting and adding numbers up to 10
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose only the one line in Minho's solution that is wrong for the first time.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s1.hint.0: Draw the 8 beads and count the red ones and the blue ones separately.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether adding the red and blue numbers that Minho said gives the same as 8 beads.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s1.line.0: The string of beads repeats 'red, blue, blue'.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s1.line.1: If you see 'red, blue, blue' as one set, the 8 beads have two sets and 2 more beads.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s1.line.2: One set has 1 red and 2 blue, so two sets have 2 red and 4 blue.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s1.line.3: The 2 extra beads are not a set, so they are not counted. So there are 2 red and 4 blue.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s1.explain: The 4th line is the first one that is wrong. The 2 beads left over at the end of the string are also beads, so they must be counted by color. The 2 left over are red and blue, so red is 2+1=3 and blue is 4+1=5. Lines 1 to 3 are correct.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s2.prompt: If you string 10 beads with the same rule, how many blue beads will there be?
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s2.hint.0: Draw the 10 beads in order and write their colors.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s2.hint.1: If there are beads left over at the end of the string, use the rule to work out what color they are.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s2.r.b: Check whether you counted the number of red beads. Count the 10 beads by color.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s2.r.c: This thinking guessed it is half of the beads. Check whether the blue and red beads are the same number.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s2.r.d: This thinking counted the bead left over at the end of the string as blue. Use the rule to check what color the leftover bead is.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s2.explain: If the set red, blue, blue comes three times, that is 9 beads, and the 10th bead is red. Red is 3+1=4 and blue is 6.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s3.prompt: String beads with the same rule, starting with red. Find three different bead counts n for which the blue beads are exactly 2 times the red beads. (There are at least 7 and at most 20 beads.)
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s3.hint.0: Change the number of beads to 7, 8, 9, ... and write in a table how many red and blue beads there are each time.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s3.hint.1: Gather the bead counts where blue is 2 times red, and look at what they have in common.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s3.ok.c1: There are at least 7 and at most 20 beads.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s3.fail.c1: Please choose a natural number from 7 to 20 for the beads.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s3.ok.c2: The blue beads are exactly 2 times the red beads.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s3.fail.c2: With this number of beads, the blue beads are not 2 times the red beads. Draw the beads and count them by color.
n-m-e1-s2b-03.s.s3.explain: When there are 9, 12, 15, or 18 beads, the string ends exactly on a set of 'red, blue, blue', so blue is 2 times red. If there are beads left after the sets, there is one more red or one more blue, so it is not 2 times.

n-m-e1-s2b-04.title: How Many Cookies Could Be Left?
n-m-e1-s2b-04.goal: In a subtraction story, follow how the range of possible values for the number left gets narrower each time one more piece of information is given, and find the boundary where two amounts become equal.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.material: There are cookies on a plate. When someone eats cookies, the number of cookies left on the plate changes. You want to find out how many cookies are left on the plate after Minji has eaten. More information is given one piece at a time.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.thinking.0: Say what you do not know yet as a range
n-m-e1-s2b-04.thinking.1: Narrow the possible numbers with new information
n-m-e1-s2b-04.thinking.2: Find the boundary where they become equal
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.prompt: Each time there is something new that you are told, choose what you can say about the cookies left.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.hint.0: Show the number of cookies at the start and the number of cookies eaten in the story, with a picture or in words.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.hint.1: Add the new information to the story, and compare whether the idea you chose before is still correct.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.0.info: There were 6 cookies on the plate. Minji ate some cookies. You do not know yet how many she ate.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: How many cookies are left on the plate?
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.0.after: If you do not know the number eaten, you cannot decide the number of cookies left as a single number. Still, you can tell that it is fewer than 6.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Minji ate, so the cookies have decreased. It cannot be 6 as before.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: I do not know how many, but fewer than 6 are left.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Once cookies are eaten, there can only be fewer. There cannot be more left than at the start.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This thinking decided that only 1 was eaten. You do not know the number eaten yet.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.1.info: It turns out there are more cookies left than cookies eaten. You still do not know the number of cookies eaten.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: How many cookies could be left?
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If 1 cookie was eaten, 5 are left, and if 2 were eaten, 4 are left, so more are left than eaten. If 3 are eaten, the number left is also 3, so they are the same. So the number of cookies left is 4 or 5.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If 3 cookies are left, 3 cookies were eaten too, so there are not more left than eaten.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: If 1 cookie is left, 5 cookies were eaten. Check whether more are left than eaten.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This thinking did not use the new information that was given.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: How many cookies are left? Also check whether it fits what you found before.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If you eat 2 from 6, 4 are left. 4 is inside the '4 or 5' found before, so the statements agree with each other.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Check whether you mixed it up with the case where 3 were eaten.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: If 5 are left, 1 cookie was eaten.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This thinking added 2 to 6. When cookies are eaten, there are fewer.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s1.reflect: At first, you only knew that fewer than 6 cookies were left. As each new piece of information was added, the possible number narrowed to 4 or 5, and once you knew the number of cookies eaten, it was decided as one number. Tell how your thinking narrowed each time more information was given.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s2.prompt: This time there are 10 cookies on the plate. Minji ate at least 1, and there are more cookies left than cookies eaten. Choose the number of cookies eaten a and the number of cookies left b in three different ways.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s2.hint.0: Decide on a number of cookies eaten, and work out how many are left if that many are eaten from 10.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s2.hint.1: Put the number left and the number eaten side by side and compare which is greater.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the cookies eaten a natural number that is at least 1, and the cookies left a number that is at least 0.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The cookies eaten and the cookies left add up to 10.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The cookies eaten and the cookies left must add up to the 10 cookies at the start.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s2.ok.c3: There are more cookies left than cookies eaten.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s2.fail.c3: There are not more cookies left than cookies eaten.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s2.explain: When 1, 2, 3, or 4 cookies are eaten, 9, 8, 7, or 6 are left, so more are left. If 5 are eaten, 5 are left too, so there are not more left.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s3.prompt: Out of 10 cookies, for there to be more cookies left than cookies eaten, what must the number of cookies eaten be? (At least 1 cookie is eaten.)
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s3.hint.0: Increase the number of cookies eaten one at a time from 1, and write in a table how the number left changes.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s3.hint.1: Find when the cookies left and the cookies eaten become the same.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s3.r.a: If 5 cookies are eaten, 5 are left too, so they are the same.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s3.r.b: If more cookies are eaten, fewer are left. Check how many are left if 6 are eaten.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s3.o.c: It only has to be less than 10.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s3.r.c: If 9 are eaten, only 1 cookie is left.
n-m-e1-s2b-04.s.s3.explain: If 1, 2, 3, or 4 cookies are eaten, more are left; if 5, they are equal; if 6 or more, fewer are left. So fewer than 5 must be eaten. The boundary is 5, which splits 10 into two equal parts.

n-m-e1-s2b-05.title: Take Out First, or Put In First?
n-m-e1-s2b-05.goal: Learn that when the order of adding and subtracting changes, a story can become impossible, and make a story yourself that becomes possible when you change the order.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.material: Harin plays a game of putting balls into a box and taking them out. There are 3 balls in the box. The game is made of two jobs: 'take out 5 balls' and 'put in 6 balls'. Whether the game can be played depends on which job is done first.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.thinking.0: Think about the order in which things happen
n-m-e1-s2b-05.thinking.1: Recognize a case that cannot be done (not enough balls to take out)
n-m-e1-s2b-05.thinking.2: Make a story that fits the conditions yourself
n-m-e1-s2b-05.prereq.0: Addition and subtraction with numbers up to 10
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.prompt: There are 3 balls in the box. Can the game below be played 'in this order'? Game: take out 5 balls, and then put in 6 balls.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.hint.0: Put out 3 balls and play the game in its order. First check whether you can do the first job.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.hint.1: Before doing the second job, count how many balls are in the box.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.o.a: It cannot be done. There are only 3 balls in the box, so you cannot take out 5 first.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.o.b: It can be done. You subtract 5 from 3 and add 6.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.r.b: You cannot take 5 balls out of a box that has only 3. Actually put out 3 balls and try taking out 5.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.o.c: It cannot be done. Taking out and putting in cannot be done together.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.r.c: Putting in after taking out can be done separately. Look at where the problem is.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.o.d: It can be done. There are 6 balls to put in, so it is fine.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.r.d: Putting in is done after taking out. Look at how many balls are in the box when you take out.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s1.explain: At the moment you take balls out, there are only 3 in the box, so you cannot take out 5. Putting in is a job done after that, so it does not help.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s2.prompt: Shall we change the order? There are 3 balls in the box. If you first put in 6 balls and then take out 5 balls, how many balls are left in the box?
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put out 3 balls, and after putting in 6, first write the number of balls in the box.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s2.hint.1: From that number, cross out as many as you take out, and count the balls left.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s2.r.a: This thinking did 5-3, subtracting the smaller number from the larger. First count how many balls are in the box after putting balls in.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s2.r.b: You did not count the 6 balls put in. First find the number of balls after putting in 6.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s2.r.d: This thinking added 3, 6, and 5 all together. When you take out, there are fewer balls.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s2.explain: If you put 6 balls in with 3, you get 9, and if you take 5 out of 9, 4 are left. Even with the same numbers, as in 3+6-5, changing the order can make the game possible.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.prompt: There are a balls in the box. Make three different cases where the game of taking out b balls and then putting in c balls cannot be played, but if you change the order, first putting in c and then taking out b, it can. After finishing in the changed order, at least 1 ball must be left. (a, b, and c are all at least 1 and at most 20)
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.hint.0: Decide the number of balls at the start, a, and choose a number greater than a for the number of balls taken out, b.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.hint.1: After you decide the number of balls put in, c, work out how many balls there are after putting them in first, and how many are left if you take out b from there.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.var.a: Number of balls at the start a
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.var.b: Number of balls taken out b
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.var.c: Number of balls put in c
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.ok.c1: All three numbers are at least 1 and at most 20.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make a, b, and c all numbers from 1 to 20.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.ok.c2: More balls are taken out than there were at the start, so it cannot be done if you take out first.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.fail.c2: The number taken out must be greater than the number of balls in the box at the start, so that 'taking out first' cannot be done.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.ok.c3: If you put in first and then take out, at least 1 ball is left.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.fail.c3: Even if you put in first, there are not enough balls to take out, or none are left. Count the number of balls after putting in again.
n-m-e1-s2b-05.s.s3.explain: For example, from a box that starts with 2, you cannot take out 4 first, but if you put in 5 first, there are 7, and after taking out 4, 3 are left. It works if the number taken out is greater than the number at the start, and the number of balls after putting in is greater than the number taken out.
